summary: Most visitors to Suriname buy an e-Tourist Card online for about USD 25 instead of a visa — it is bought before departure and allows a stay of up to 90 days — while CARICOM nationals move freely and remaining nationalities apply for an eVisa or a consular visa.

source.name: Government of Suriname — tourist card information

fee.notes: Approximate — single-entry short-stay visas cost around USD 45 and multiple-entry versions more; the exact amount is shown during the online application. Use only the official government portal, as many look-alike commercial sites charge large mark-ups.

Approximate and varies by nationality and number of entries. Applying in person is still the route for nationalities not covered by the online systems, and for anyone whose online application is referred for further checks.

Approximate — multiple-entry business visas cost more and normally require an invitation letter from the Surinamese company or institution you are visiting. A tourist card does not cover business visits, including the offshore oil sector.

passportValidity.text: Your passport should be valid for at least 6 months on arrival, and the tourist card or visa must have been issued against that same passport. A renewed passport means a new application.

vaccinations.name: Yellow fever
vaccinations.text: A yellow fever certificate is required from travelers aged 1 year and over arriving from a country with risk of transmission, including travelers who have transited such a country. Suriname is itself a risk country, so vaccination is recommended for all visitors and the certificate will be checked when you travel on to Brazil or Guyana.

source.name: Government of Suriname — Ministry of Health

vaccinations.name: Malaria prophylaxis
vaccinations.text: Not an entry requirement. Paramaribo and the coastal strip are essentially malaria-free, but the interior and the gold-mining districts are not. Take advice from a travel clinic if you are going upriver.

source.name: Government of Suriname — Ministry of Health

travelInsurance.text: Insurance is not checked at the border, but hospital care in Paramaribo must be paid for and anything serious means evacuation to Trinidad, the Netherlands or the United States — cover including medical evacuation is strongly recommended, especially for jungle trips.

onwardTicket.text: Tourist-card and visa holders should hold a confirmed return or onward ticket within the permitted stay; airlines check this before boarding for Johan Adolf Pengel International Airport.

proofOfFunds.text: No fixed amount is published, though officers may ask about your accommodation and means of support. Visa applications normally include bank statements for the period of the trip.

declarations.name: Printed tourist card or eVisa confirmation
declarations.text: Buy the tourist card or eVisa before you fly and travel with a printed copy as well as the electronic one — airline staff at check-in and the immigration desk in Paramaribo both ask to see it, and airport wi-fi is not something to rely on.

source.name: Government of Suriname — tourist card information

currencyLimits.text: Cash or negotiable instruments worth EUR 10,000 or more, or the equivalent in another currency, must be declared to customs on arrival and departure.

notes: Gold cannot simply be carried out of the country — exports are controlled and require documentation.
Wildlife products, including caiman and jaguar items and untreated feathers, are prohibited under CITES rules.
Fresh food, plants and seeds are restricted; declare anything agricultural rather than risk a penalty.

payments.text: Cards are accepted in Paramaribo's larger hotels, supermarkets and a few restaurants, but foreign cards are often declined and ATMs do not always accept them. Bring US dollars or euros in cash to change at a bank or licensed cambio, and carry Surinamese dollars for the interior, where there is no banking at all.

safety.text: Suriname is calmer than its neighbors, but street robbery happens in Paramaribo — particularly in the Palm Garden, around Waterkant after dark and in the Tourtonne area. Use taxis at night, keep valuables discreet, and treat the gold-mining districts of the interior as places to avoid.

source.name: U.S. Department of State — Suriname Travel Advisory

bestTimeToVisit.text: Suriname has two dry seasons — a short one in February and March and a long one from August to November. The long dry season is best for river trips, jungle lodges and the sea-turtle beaches at Galibi.

tips.text: Buy the e-Tourist Card before you leave home and apply only through the official government channel. Airlines will not board you without it, buying on arrival is unreliable and more expensive, and the search results are full of commercial sites charging several times the real price.

Dutch is the official language and the one used on signs and paperwork, with Sranan Tongo as the everyday lingua franca. English is widely understood in Paramaribo's tourism trade but much less so in the interior.

Carry cash. The Surinamese dollar has been through heavy devaluations, foreign cards are often refused, and prices for tours are frequently quoted in US dollars or euros. Bring clean, undamaged notes to change at a bank or cambio.

The rainforest interior — Bigi Pan, the Upper Suriname river villages, Raleighvallen — is reached by shared taxi and dugout canoe or by a small plane, and effectively has to be booked as a package. Allow a spare day either side of an international flight.

Suriname drives on the left, a legacy it shares with neighboring Guyana, and the road east into French Guiana ends at a ferry across the Marowijne river. If you plan to drive on, check the ferry timetable and the French border requirements in advance.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Suriname?
faq.answer: Most visitors do not need a full visa but do need an e-Tourist Card, bought online for around USD 25 before departure and valid for a stay of up to 90 days. It covers citizens of the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, the EU and EEA, Australia, New Zealand and many other countries. CARICOM nationals enter freely with no card, and nationalities outside the tourist-card scheme apply for an eVisa or a consular visa.

faq.question: What is the difference between the tourist card and a Surinamese visa?
faq.answer: The tourist card is a simple, cheaper entry permit for holidays only — single entry, up to 90 days, no invitation letter. A visa is required if you are visiting for business, staying longer, needing multiple entries, or if your nationality is not covered by the tourist-card scheme. Business travel on a tourist card is not permitted.

faq.question: Can I buy the Suriname tourist card on arrival?
faq.answer: Do not count on it. Airlines routinely refuse boarding to passengers without a tourist card or visa already issued, and where an on-arrival counter exists it charges more and can be closed. Buy it online in advance and carry a printout.

faq.question: Do CARICOM citizens need a tourist card for Suriname?
faq.answer: No. Suriname is a CARICOM member state, and nationals of other member states enter under Caribbean Community free-movement arrangements — normally admitted for six months without a card or visa. Carry your passport and, if relevant, your CARICOM Skills Certificate.

faq.question: Do I need a yellow fever certificate for Suriname?
faq.answer: It is required from age 1 if you are arriving from — or have transited — a country with risk of yellow fever transmission. Suriname is itself a risk country, so vaccination is recommended for everyone, and the certificate is checked when you travel on to Brazil, Guyana or French Guiana.

faq.question: Can I extend my stay in Suriname?
faq.answer: Yes, in principle. Apply to the immigration authorities in Paramaribo before your permitted stay runs out; extensions are usually granted in short blocks and require your accommodation details and onward ticket. It is simpler to buy the full 90-day tourist card up front than to extend later.
